extracted.intended_audience: classical philologists / textual critics preparing or evaluating critical editions of ancient Greek texts (e.g., Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and evaluative criteria for establishing the relationships, readings, and genealogy of manuscripts of a classical text (here: Aristotle's Poetics). Emphasises internal/external evidence, palaeography, translations, editorial conjecture, and chronological/provenance reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing internal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Convincing internal evidence would be the occurrence in all MSS. of defects traceable to A only, e.g. the loss of words caused by rents in its material or blots on its pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared physical or textual defects that can be directly attributed to a particular exemplar (e.g. identical losses, blanks, or corruptions across all descendants) count as strong internal evidence that they descend from that exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing external evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Convincing external evidence would be the statement of a good authority to the effect that A was the first MS. of the book brought to Western Europe, and statements of other good authorities connecting the other MSS. with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative documentary testimony (ownership records, purchase histories, statements by trustworthy authorities) linking manuscripts to an archetype provides strong external support for genealogical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic inference from provenance and history
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct (internal or external) evidence is lacking, one must 'consider the probabilities' — e.g. owner histories, dispersal events (fall of Constantinople), known purchases or looting — to infer likely manuscript transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known historical events, owners, dates and likely movements of libraries to assess plausibility of transmission scenarios; treat such inferences as probabilistic rather than conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological/dating constraints on derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: If all other MSS are copies of A, they or their ancestors must have been made in Constantinople before the fall of the city, or in Latin Europe after its fall; hence we should expect the earliest dated MS. (1457) to be derived directly from A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare dates of extant manuscripts with hypothesised transmission events; if the chronology leaves insufficient time for the development of distinct recensions, the hypothesis is improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shared readings/blanks/variants to infer kinship
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement in peculiar readings, blanks, or the same corruptions among manuscripts can indicate common ancestry (e.g., D and d; Guelferbytanus as copy of Par. 2040).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique or systematic agreements (including identical omissions or marginal insertions) are used to group MSS; require caution when other MSS or intermediaries may have been consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about declaring direct copying
rubrics_metrics.description: The cases in which we can declare existing MSS. to be copies of other existing MSS. without any hesitation are rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when there is unambiguous evidence (unique shared errors, clear history) should one assert direct copying; otherwise favour hypotheses of shared archetype or intermediate exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of scribal practice (mechanical copying vs editing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scribes often copied mechanically and quickly (e.g., Ruosus copying many works in months); scribes generally 'felt no responsibility' to emend, so many fifteenth-century scribes are unlikely to have produced bold emendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate time, professional context, and scribe's reported behaviour to judge whether a manuscript is likely to contain original emendations or merely reproduce its exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conjectural emendation from manuscript evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Lascaris’s conjectures and marginal emendations were bold and later entered editions; conjectures must be distinguished from readings supported by MSS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the apparatus and in establishing the text, mark and weigh conjectures separately; track when conjectures entered printed editions and subsequent MSS via marginalia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for printed editions and intermediate editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed editions (e.g., Aldine editio princeps) and translators (e.g., Valla) have specific bases in MSS and have influenced later corrections and marginalia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace influence of printed editions on later MSS (marginal corrections, copied emendations) and avoid assuming readings in later MSS are independent if they may derive from a printed source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent translations/versions as an external test
rubrics_metrics.description: The test proposed is the Arabic Version; agreement in any considerable matter with that document on the part of a Greek MS. against A may be regarded as evidence of independence of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare readings with independent versions (Arabic, Syriac, translations) — agreements that contradict a putative parent MS support independent lineages; use glossaries and translation correspondences to interpret equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight unlikely shared corruptions highly
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared corruptions that involve complex errors (e.g., 'involves three itacisms') are unlikely to have occurred more than once and thus strongly indicate a common source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identical improbable corruptions appear in multiple MSS, treat them as strong evidence of dependence rather than coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret omissions with attention to plausibility and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Omissions (e.g., omission of a negative in a definition) occurring in several MSS and the Arabic can be accidental or intentional (possibly a Christian scribe omitting a phrase on moral grounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether omissions are palaeographic accidents or deliberate changes by scribes/editors, using context, doctrinal plausibility, and parallel evidence in translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palaeographic mechanism analysis for corruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many corruptions can be explained by script confusions (e.g., confusion of x with vc, transposition of consonants, uncial vs cursive forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain variant readings by reference to plausible letter confusions, itacisms, dittography, or misread strokes appropriate to the hands and scripts involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cross-work doctrinal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The true reading may be learned from what the author says elsewhere (compare with Politics, Natural History, etc.) to decide between variant readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the author’s known concepts and parallel passages across works to judge which variant coheres best with the author’s doctrine and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect influence of later hands and marginal corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Marginal corrections of various MSS seem to be the work of readers who consulted the Aldine edition; such corrections may be by later scholars (e.g., Pazzi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine margins and later hands to identify readings introduced post-exemplum; these should not be treated as witnesses to the archetype without independent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate improbable additions (e.g., lists) critically
rubrics_metrics.description: A list such as the 'five substantives' could be an easy later addition; the absence of expected parallel additions (e.g., sigma in masculine terminations) makes such an addition suspicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge added material by its ease of insertion and by internal consistency: if an addition would logically entail other additions that are absent, suspect later interpolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group manuscripts by characteristic readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify manuscript groups (e.g., Ennoian Group, Mimesis Group, Group of the Five Substantives) according to recurring characteristic readings specific to that group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define groups by clusters of shared distinctive readings; list the characteristic variants that name or typify each group and use them to classify other MSS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement on erroneous readings indicates kinship
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of proving kinship between MSS it is not necessary that the reading on which they agree should be sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared obvious errors or corruptions are valuable genealogical markers; use them as evidence of relationship even if they do not represent the original text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to multiple possible models and non-uniqueness of derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent agreements may be due to consultation of several exemplars or common use of a now-lost archetype rather than direct copying from one surviving MS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for collational practices (scribes consulting more than one exemplar), lost intermediaries, and shared archetypes when explaining mixed readings; avoid oversimplified parent-child attributions.
